**Where we are ahead:** against the Zig implementations whose READMEs we read: the ML-KEM-768/X25519 hybrid KEX plus curve25519, NIST ECDH P-256/P-384/P-521, DH group-exchange and DH group14/16, rsa-sha2 and P-256/P-384/P-521 host keys, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and AES-GCM ciphers, RFC 8308 `server-sig-algs`, server role included (misshod: one algorithm of each kind; sshz README states no algorithm list, so its algorithm set is unchecked) · **Where we are behind:** no SFTP, no certificates or `ssh-agent`, no X11/agent forwarding, no server-side TCP/IP forwarding (the server owns no sockets by design), no legacy SHA-1/CBC opt-ins yet (the non-legacy algorithm menu matches Go's), and server handlers that are one-shot callbacks (a "shell" served here is batch, not a pty driving a process) (see *What is deliberately not done* and *Backlog / deferred*); sshz advertises agent forwarding and Dropbear/libssh interop besides.

## Design & invariants

- **Scope: the whole client/server path to running a remote command.** RFC 4253 transport (part 1,
  `transport.zig` + `server.zig`), RFC 4252 user authentication (part 2, `userauth.zig`) and the
  RFC 4254 connection protocol (part 3, `connection.zig`), all implemented for **both roles**.
  There are no `@panic` stubs left in this module.
- **`aes{128,192,256}-ctr` (RFC 4344) keep ONE 128-bit counter per direction across packets**; a packet's
  keystream is `aes192.ctrXor` over the context (pipeline width of std's AES block, two-`u64` counter: std's
  `modes.ctr` writes the counter byte by byte on Zig 0.17, #36256), 0.15× the time of the one-block-per-call
  loop it replaced at 1504 bytes (`tools/ctr_bench.zig` is the A/B program, header says how to build it). Test: equals
  std's `modes.ctr` over a counter that runs on across packet-sized calls and wraps, for all three key sizes.
- **Layering mirrors the RFCs themselves:** version exchange (§4.2) → KEXINIT algorithm negotiation
  (§7.1) → key exchange → SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS both ways → the Binary Packet Protocol (§6) carries every
  subsequent message, in the clear before NEWKEYS and encrypted after — through the *same*
  `readPacket`/`writePacket` entry points either way, keyed on a `CipherState` that is `.none`
  during KEX and a real cipher afterward. Userauth and channels add **no framing and no crypto of
  their own**: `userauth.zig`/`connection.zig` contain only message encode/decode and protocol
  state, sent through `Transport.sendPacket`/`recvPacket`. Client (`clientHandshake`) and server
  (`serverHandshake`) drive the same layering; the server reuses `transport.zig`'s packet codec,
  `KexInit` and `deriveKeys` rather than duplicating them.
- **One decoder for peer input (`messages.Cursor`).** Every message parser in the module — KEX,
  userauth, channels — decodes with the same bounds-checked cursor: `string`/`byte`/`boolean`/
  `uint32`, each checked against the buffer it was built from. An attacker-controlled `uint32`
  length can therefore only ever produce `error.ProtocolError`; it can never index out of bounds,
  panic, or size an allocation — **above the KEX layer**. `KexInit.decode` is the
  exception and the one an auditor meets first: it predates the cursor and reads its ten
  name-lists through `readListOwned` → `messages.readString`, where a peer's `uint32` DOES
  size a `gpa.alloc` and the error is `StringTooLarge`/`EndOfStream`. That allocation is
  capped at `max_wire_string_len` (1 MiB), only one is live at a time, and an over-announced
  length fails `readSliceAll` and is freed by the `errdefer` — so it is bounded, not
  unbounded. Stated because an invariant an auditor is invited to rely on should not have a
  silent exception in the first message of every connection. (`transport.zig`'s `SliceReader` and `server.zig`'s `WireCursor`
  are aliases of it, not copies.)
- **Wire-format codec (`messages.zig`):** `writeString`/`readString` (RFC 4251 §5 length-prefixed
  byte string), `writeMpint`/`readMpint` (§5 mpint, including the high-bit-set-implies-leading-
  zero-byte rule), `writeNameList`/`readNameList` (§5 comma-joined name-list), the RFC 4253 §12 /
  4252 §6 / 4254 §9 message numbers, and `Cursor`.
- **Transport-agnostic:** `Transport` takes an already-connected `std.Io.Reader`/`std.Io.Writer`
  pair, same shape as the sibling `opcua` module's `Connection` — this module never opens a socket
  itself, and never spawns a process (see the server-side `CommandHandler` seam below).
- **Algorithm lists are runtime-configurable (Go `Config.KeyExchanges/Ciphers/MACs`,
  `ClientConfig.HostKeyAlgorithms`).** `transport.Algorithms` (`kex`, `host_keys`,
  `ciphers`, `macs`, most-preferred first) sits on `Transport.algorithms` (client: set before
  `clientHandshake`) and `ServerConfig.algorithms` (server); every exchange of the connection,
  re-exchanges included, offers and negotiates from it. Defaults are `kex_algorithms`
  (mlkem768x25519-sha256, curve25519-sha256 + `@libssh.org`, ecdh-sha2-nistp256/384/521,
  diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256, diffie-hellman-group14-sha256/group16-sha512), `server_host_key_algorithms` (ssh-ed25519, rsa-sha2-256/512,
  ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521), `encryption_algorithms` (chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com, aes256-ctr,
  aes256-gcm@openssh.com, aes128-gcm@openssh.com, aes128-ctr, aes192-ctr), `mac_algorithms`
  (hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com, hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com, hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-512 —
  Go's order); the ceiling is
  the `supported_*` lists (equal today; a legacy opt-in will live only there). `Algorithms.validate`
  refuses an empty list, a duplicate, or a name outside `supported_*` with
  `error.UnsupportedAlgorithm` before anything is sent — the RFC 8308 and strict-KEX indicators are
  outside `supported_kex_algorithms`, so they cannot be configured as methods either. Negotiated
  names are canonicalised to the module's constants (`canonicalName`), so `Transport.negotiated`
  never points into a caller's list. A server's host-key list is the keys it holds, not
  `Algorithms.host_keys`. `compression_algorithms` stays `none` only. `ServerConfig.server_sig_algs`
  (below) is narrowable downward.
- **RFC 8308 extension negotiation, both roles.** The client appends `ext-info-c` and the server
  `ext-info-s` to the `kex_algorithms` they *send* (§2.1); `transport.kex_algorithms`, the list both
  sides negotiate against, never contains either, so §2.2's "if these names become negotiated as key
  exchange methods, the parties MUST disconnect" is structurally unreachable rather than checked at
  runtime. A server that saw `ext-info-c` sends `SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO` carrying `server-sig-algs` (§3.1)
  as the first packet after its `SSH_MSG_NEWKEYS` — §2.4's first opportunity, which is the one that
  matters: a client chooses its signature algorithm before its first `SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST`. A
  client that did not advertise the indicator is sent **nothing**, not an empty message, because to
  such a peer message 7 is an unknown transport message. Both roles accept a peer's
  `SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO` at both §2.4 opportunities and ignore extensions they do not implement (§2.5);
  this module sends none as a client.
  **Why it is load-bearing rather than cosmetic:** an `ssh-rsa` key blob names no hash, so
  `rsa-sha2-256` and `rsa-sha2-512` are both valid for it and a client that is not told will not
  guess — real `ssh` logs `send_pubkey_test: no mutual signature algorithm` and never offers the key.
  `ssh-ed25519` and `ecdsa-sha2-nistp256` each have exactly one name and were never affected.
  What a server advertises is `ServerConfig.server_sig_algs`, defaulting to
  `transport.public_key_algorithms` — the four names `serveUserauth` can verify, pinned to
  `keyBlobTypeFor`/`verifySignature` by a test in both directions. A caller whose own
  `AuthorizedKeyCheck` is stricter **narrows** it; widening it would advertise a name the hook then
  refuses, leaving a client with one failed attempt and no second choice. Verification is *not*
  restricted to the advertised list — §3.1 explicitly allows a client to use an algorithm not in it.
  Client side, `userauth.authenticatePublickey` picks the strongest name the server accepts for the
  key's type from `Transport.server_sig_algs`, falling back to the key's own name when the server
  sent no extension (§3.1: a client "MUST NOT make any assumptions" then).
- **Host-key trust is entirely the caller's concern (client side).** `HostKeyVerifier` is a
  caller-supplied policy; `knownhosts.zig` supplies ready-made verifiers (`KnownHosts` over
  known_hosts text the caller read, `FixedHostKey` for pinning), but this module never reads a
  known_hosts file and has no TOFU policy.
  Symmetrically, **user-key trust is the caller's concern on the server side**:
  `userauth.AuthorizedKeyCheck` is the one-line-of-`authorized_keys` seam, and this module never
  reads the filesystem for it. What it does give both sides is the **text formats**: `keys.zig`
  parses and writes `authorized_keys` lines and fingerprints keys (`findAuthorizedKey` is the body of
  a typical `AuthorizedKeyCheck`), over text the caller read.
- **Every caller-supplied policy carries a `ctx: *anyopaque` and is called through it.**
  `transport.HostKeyVerifier`, `userauth.AuthorizedKeyCheck`, `userauth.PasswordCheck` and
  `connection.CommandHandler` are `{ ctx, fn(ctx, …) }` structs, not bare `*const fn`. A process
  holding several connections gives each its own policy state without a global, which is what Go's
  `HostKeyCallback` closure and russh's `check_server_key` handler method also do. ⚠ Every slice
  handed to such a callback is borrowed for the duration of that call only — notably
  `HostKeyInfo.key_blob`, which points into the handshake's packet scratch; a callback that keeps
  one must copy it.
- **A refusal says why, to the caller — never to the peer.** `transport.HostKeyPolicy.failure` and
  `userauth.AuthConfig.failure` are optional out-pointers (the idiom `sntp` uses for its
  Kiss-o'-Death code) filled in with a `HostKeyFailure` / `AuthFailure` before the corresponding
  error is returned. They exist because an error set cannot carry a payload and one
  `error.HostKeyVerificationFailed` covered four different situations — unknown host, changed key,
  revoked key, user declined — plus this module's own signature/algorithm refusals. Nothing about
  them reaches the wire: RFC 4252 §5.1's SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE still carries no reason at all
  (see "Known limits" below), deliberately. `AuthConfig.failure` is written on EVERY rejected
  credential, not only the one that ultimately ends the call, so it is valid to read after ANY
  error `serveUserauth` returns — not only `error.AuthenticationFailed` — as long as at least one
  credential was actually rejected first (A1/examples/ssh.md S2: a peer that closes the connection
  after one rejected credential makes the call return `error.EndOfStream` instead, and `failure`
  already holds the right answer). `AuthConfig.on_rejected` is the unambiguous alternative: it
  fires at the moment of each rejection, so a caller never has to guess whether `failure` was
  touched at all.
- **Userauth key material is the same union as host keys.** `userauth.AuthKey == server.HostKey`:
  the wire formats for "a public key blob plus a signature made by it" are identical whether the
  key authenticates a host during KEX or a user during RFC 4252, so `publicBlob`/`sign`/
  `algorithmName`/`fromOpenSSH` and `transport.verifySignature` are reused verbatim by both. Key
  algorithms wired end-to-end for userauth: **ssh-ed25519** (RFC 8709), **rsa-sha2-256** and
  **rsa-sha2-512** (RFC 8332 — the signature algorithm name differs from the `ssh-rsa` key-blob
  type, and the module enforces that pairing), **ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521** (RFC 5656). Bare `ssh-rsa`
  (SHA-1) is deliberately **not** accepted.
- **A key is never copied.** `HostKey` holds the private key by value (rsa ≈ 12 KiB),
  so it lives in the caller's storage and every API takes `*const HostKey`; `fromOpenSSH` and the
  container parsers write through an out-param (zeroed on error). The rsa-sha2 hash chosen from
  `server-sig-algs` is passed beside the key (`signWithHash`/`algorithmNameFor`), not by re-tagging
  a copy. Signing and loading run one frame down and zero the stack they dirtied (`burn.zig`);
  `stackprobe_test.zig` (ReleaseFast) checks every key type for 0 residue.
- **Auth orchestration is a state machine in each role, shaped after Go `x/crypto/ssh`.** *Server* (`serveUserauth`): the enabled methods of the current step are an
  `Active` set — each method either a yes/no hook (`AuthConfig.authorized_key`/`password`/
  `keyboard_interactive`, unchanged) or a deciding callback (`AuthConfig.callbacks`, Go's
  `ServerAuthCallbacks`) returning a `Decision`: `.reject`, `.accept` with `Permissions`, or
  `.partial = *const AuthCallbacks` (Go `PartialSuccessError{Next}`). A partial success sends
  FAILURE with `partial success` = TRUE listing only `next`'s methods, replaces the active set
  with `next`, records the method in `AuthResult.completed`, locks the user name (a change is
  `ProtocolError` + DISCONNECT, as in Go/OpenSSH) and costs no attempt. Permissions are not
  carried across steps — the union makes "permissions with a partial" unrepresentable, which Go
  checks at run time. Counting is Go's: a *failure* budget (`max_attempts`, default 6 =
  OpenSSH `MaxAuthTries`, the client's first `none` free) and a *request* budget
  (`max_auth_requests` = 128 over every USERAUTH_REQUEST, queries and partials included).
  `none` succeeds only under `no_client_auth` (optionally decided by `no_client_auth_callback`)
  and never after a partial success. Keyboard-interactive runs any number of rounds through a
  `KbdPrompter` the callback drives (Go's `KeyboardInteractiveChallenge`); a round answered with
  the wrong count, malformed, or past `max_kbd_rounds` makes `challenge` false and the attempt
  a refusal whatever the callback returns. A client that sends a new USERAUTH_REQUEST instead of
  an INFO_RESPONSE abandons the dialogue (RFC 4252 §5 "MUST abandon the previous attempt"): the
  attempt counts as `wrong_answers`, no FAILURE is sent for it, and the new request is served —
  where Go reports an unexpected message and drops it (once `max_attempts` is reached the
  pending request is dropped unserved). A keyboard-interactive callback's `.accept`/`.partial`
  counts only after at least one completed round (else `error.InvalidAuthConfig`: an accept
  without a dialogue is a policy bug), and the callback runs under `userauth.kbd_burn` (its frames
  hold the answers). A configuration that cannot work (no method, hook fields and `callbacks`
  mixed — even for different methods, since a hook-enabled method is active in step 1 and would
  let a client skip a `callbacks` chain — or a `partial` whose `next` enables nothing) is
  `error.InvalidAuthConfig`. `ServeConfig.fromAuth` copies user and permissions together. `Permissions` (critical options, extensions, `extra`) are borrowed
  from the callback's `ctx` and travel `AuthResult.permissions` → `ServeConfig.permissions` →
  `RequestInfo.permissions`; the one this module enforces is `source-address` (as Go does; Go's
  other one, `no-touch-required`, is for security keys, which this module does not accept).
  **The peer address is handed in** (`AuthConfig.remote_address`/`local_address`, Go's
  `ConnMetadata.RemoteAddr`/`LocalAddr`; the module never sees the socket) and reaches every callback in
  `AuthRequest`. `source-address` is Go's `checkSourceAddressCriticalOption`: a comma list of
  addresses and CIDR blocks (`netaddr`), checked on the grant that would log the user in, for every
  method, and on a `publickey` callback's grant before PK_OK (a query fails too, before the client
  signs); no address, an empty value or an entry that parses as neither refuses
  (`AuthFailure.source_address_denied`); an IPv4-mapped peer matches as IPv4; host bits in a block are
  ignored as Go's `ParseCIDR` does (OpenSSH refuses such an entry).
  **Go's other server hooks:** `banner_callback` (Go `BannerCallback`: asked once, at the first request,
  instead of the static `banner` — both set is `InvalidAuthConfig`), `pre_auth` (Go
  `PreAuthConnCallback`: at entry, with `PreAuthConn.sendBanner`; valid for the call only, where Go's
  value may be kept until authentication ends), `on_auth` (Go `AuthLogCallback`: every verdict —
  accepted, partial, rejected with its reason — with the method name; not a successful §7 query, as
  in Go) and `publickey_verified` (Go `VerifiedPublicKeyCallback`: after the signature verified, with
  the grant that accepted the key; its `Decision` is the verdict; while it is set a `publickey`
  callback answering `partial` is `InvalidAuthConfig`, Go's "invalid library usage").
  **`hostbased` (RFC 4252 §9), both roles** (OpenSSH has both; Go neither): server
  `AuthConfig.hostbased` (yes/no) or `AuthCallbacks.hostbased` over a `HostbasedRequest` (client host
  with one trailing '.' stripped as `sshd` does, client user, algorithm, host key blob), then the host
  key's signature over `signedBlobHostbased` with this transport's session id; a refusal is
  `unauthorized_host`. Whether the name belongs to the peer address and the key to the host
  (`sshd`'s reverse DNS and `ssh_known_hosts`) is the hook's. Client `ClientMethod.hostbased` (the host
  key, host name sent as given, client user).
  **§8 password change, client side** (OpenSSH `ssh` and libssh2 have it; Go does not):
  `PasswordOptions`/`ClientAuthOptions.password_change` (`PasswordChanger`, libssh2's callback shape)
  answers SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_PASSWD_CHANGEREQ with `TRUE, old, new`, asked again when the server
  refuses the new one (at most `max_password_changes`); without it a change request stays
  `error.UnsupportedAuthMethod`. The server refuses a change request (`wrong_password`).
  *Client* (`authenticateWith`, Go `clientAuthenticate`): `none` first; then the first of the
  caller's `ClientMethod`s that the server's latest FAILURE lists and that has not failed
  (caller's order, as Go `Auth` and OpenSSH `PreferredAuthentications`); a partial success does
  not mark the method tried (OpenSSH `publickey,publickey` wants a second key). `publickey` walks
  its keys, signs only after a PK_OK that names the same blob and a matching type, and stops when
  the server no longer lists `publickey`; `retryable` repeats a plain failure up to `max_tries`
  while the server still lists the method, but never after a *declined* step (a
  `password_prompt` returning null — nothing sent — or a responder giving up);
  `max_client_auth_steps` (64) bounds the loop.
  `AuthProgress` reports allowed/partial/tried/succeeded. The FAILURE name-list is decoded into a
  `MethodSet` (names this module does not implement are dropped), so no peer string is kept.
- **Sequence numbers are `u32`** (RFC 4253 §6.4), one per direction, wrapping, carried on the
  `CipherState` payload (the plaintext `NoneState` included, so every packet of the initial
  exchange counts — a discarded wrongly-guessed KEX packet too). A rekey installs the next cipher
  with the running number, or with 0 when OpenSSH strict KEX is in force (`Transport.strict_kex`:
  both sides advertised `kex-strict-*-v00@openssh.com`; it is the Terrapin countermeasure). The
  `max_packets_per_direction` stop counts packets per key (`under_key`), far above the automatic
  rekey threshold.
- **Transport duties live in `Transport.recvPacket`/`sendPacket`** (RFC 4253 §9, §11): IGNORE,
  DEBUG and UNIMPLEMENTED are absorbed; a message number no layer implements (outside the named
  `MessageType` tags and the 60-79 userauth range) is answered SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED with its
  sequence number; a peer's KEXINIT runs a whole re-exchange in this transport's role before the
  call reads on; `rekey()` and the `rekey_limit_bytes`/`_packets` thresholds start one. Packets the
  peer sends before answering OUR KEXINIT are queued (bounded by `max_pending_bytes`) and returned
  in order. A client re-exchange requires the first exchange's host key (SHA-256 of `K_S`); the
  caller's policy is not asked again. Userauth and channels see none of it.
- **Channel flow control is real, not decorative** (RFC 4254 §5.2). Each side tracks the peer's
  remaining window and its own; a sender never emits more than `min(peer window, peer maximum
  packet size, max_send_chunk)` in one packet and blocks for SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_WINDOW_ADJUST when the
  window is exhausted; a receiver credits the peer back once half its advertised window has been
  consumed. On receipt both §5.2 limits are enforced: data beyond the granted window is
  `error.WindowOverrun` and a chunk larger than the advertised `maximum packet size` is
  `error.PacketTooLarge` — refused, not buffered.
- **The Ed25519 seed is checked against the public key in every optimize mode.** `parseEd25519Body`
  derives the pair with `Ed25519.KeyPair.generateDeterministic(seed)` and compares its public key with
  the container's copy; std's `KeyPair.fromSecretKey` re-derives it only under runtime safety, so in
  ReleaseFast/ReleaseSmall it would compare the container's copy with itself. A seed that does not
  derive the container's public key is `error.InvalidPrivateKey`.
- **The host-key PEM is walked and decoded without secret-dependent branches.** `pemDecodeOpensshBlock`
  walks the blocks with `keycodec.pem` (a malformed block of another label before the key is skipped,
  as Go's `pem.Decode` does; a broken `OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY` block is `InvalidPem` even when a good one
  follows; the first block in the text is used) and decodes the body with `b64ct` straight into the
  caller's wiped buffer: no skip table, no alphabet table, no stripped copy on the stack. Errors:
  `MissingPemBlock`, `InvalidPem` (also for a body that decodes past the 16 KiB buffer).
- **The DH exponent goes through montint, not `std.crypto.ff`.** `dhPowModPrime` is montint's `powMont`
  (fixed 5-bit windows, branchless table gather) with a branchless exponent loader: `ff`'s window select
  compiles to a conditional jump in ReleaseFast, which leaked the exponent's windows. Group exchange
  (`gexPow`) uses the same kernel on `GexMod`.
- **Secrets do not stay on the stack.** The per-method KEX entry points take `out: *KexResult` and burn
  their bodies (std's X25519, the `mlkem` module's ML-KEM and the modexp frames included); the KEX rounds, `installCipher`,
  `deriveKeys` and `writePacket`/`readPacket` burn theirs (`burn.zig`). `stackprobe_test.zig` and
  `stackprobe2_test.zig` probe each method and role and a whole handshake per role for residue.
- **Public keys and `known_hosts` (`keys.zig`, `knownhosts.zig`).** `PublicKey.parse`/`verify`/`eql`,
  `fingerprintSha256`/`fingerprintMd5` (byte-equal to `ssh-keygen -lf`), the `authorized_keys` line
  parser (quoted options), `AuthorizedKeysIterator`, `findAuthorizedKey` and `writeAuthorizedKey` work
  over text the caller read. RSA keys above the `rsa` module's 4096-bit cap are skipped as unusable
  (OpenSSH goes to 16384). `knownhosts.check` decides in OpenSSH's order: `@revoked` -> accept ->
  same-type mismatch -> unknown; wildcards, negation, `[host]:port` and hashed `|1|` entries
  (byte-equal to `ssh-keygen -H`) are matched; `writeLine` writes a plain or hashed line. A
  `@cert-authority` line is parsed and never treated as a host key.
- **Algorithm menu.** Besides the defaults above, the cipher/MAC set is Go's non-legacy set; host and
  user keys cover ed25519, rsa-sha2-256/512 and ecdsa nistp256/384/521 (loading, signing, verifying;
  passphrase-protected ed25519 and ecdsa-p256 OpenSSH keys load; a wrong or missing passphrase is refused). Group exchange: the client takes any
  server prime of 2048..8192 bits (the build option below caps it), the server answers from the fixed
  group14/group16 primes as Go's does.

## Threat model / out of scope

Implemented and live-interop-verified against real OpenSSH in both directions (see Verification),
so the security properties below are in effect, not aspirational.

1. **Exchange hash / host-key authentication (part 1).** `H` is computed and verified exactly per
   RFC 8731 §4 / RFC 4253 §8 (client verifies the server's signature over `H`; server signs `H`).
   `HostKeyPolicy.verifier`'s verdict gates whether the client proceeds — a caller that always
   answers `.accept` has no host-key security at all, but that is a caller-policy choice this
   module deliberately does not make. The verifier is given the host and port the caller dialled
   (`HostKeyInfo.host`/`.port`) precisely so that answering it *properly* — a known_hosts lookup —
   does not require the caller to smuggle them in through a global.
2. **Userauth session-id binding (part 2) — the load-bearing new property.** The RFC 4252 §7
   `publickey` signature is computed over `string session_id || byte 50 || string user || string
   service || string "publickey" || boolean TRUE || string alg || string key_blob` and nothing
   else. `userauth.signedBlob` is the *single* encoder used by both the signer and the verifier, so
   the two cannot drift. The verifier always takes the session id from **its own** `Transport`,
   never from anything on the wire; the signer takes it from its own transport too
   (`authenticatePublickeyBoundTo` exists solely so the negative test can sign against a wrong one
   and watch it be rejected). Because the session id is the first KEX's exchange hash — unique per
   connection, unforgeable by a third party — a signature captured on one connection cannot be
   replayed onto another. A subtle way to lose this property is to hand the verifier a slice into a
   *copy* of the session id rather than the transport's own storage: it compiles, and it silently
   binds the signature to stack garbage. That exact bug was made and fixed during development and
   is pinned by a regression test (`sessionId borrows from the transport`).
3. **The connection protocol is unreachable before authentication.** `serveUserauth` treats any
   non-SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST message (notably SSH_MSG_CHANNEL_OPEN) as `error.ProtocolError`,
   sends SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT and returns; the caller only reaches `serveSession` after a successful
   `AuthResult`. Failed attempts are counted and capped (`AuthConfig.max_attempts`).
4. **Peer-controlled lengths cannot panic or over-allocate.** All decoding goes through
   `messages.Cursor` (bounds-checked, typed errors); every peer string has an explicit cap
   (`max_user_len`, `max_key_blob_len`, `max_signature_len`, …); channel data is capped by the
   advertised window *and* by the caller's `max_output`/`max_input`. The Binary Packet Protocol
   caps `packet_length` at `messages.max_wire_string_len` (1 MiB).
5. **Not covered / caller's job.** Constant-time password comparison and rate limiting belong in
   the `PasswordCheck` callback. The `password` method sends the secret inside an encrypted packet;
   both roles scrub the heap buffer that holds the plaintext (the client its request buffer, the
   server `serveUserauth`'s packet scratch — see "Known limits" below for why that scrub is load-
   bearing only in unsafe optimize modes), but neither can scrub `writePacket`'s internal
   stack buffer — a stack-secret-residue concern shared with every other message. OAEP/
   Bleichenbacher-style timing leaks are the `rsa` module's concern. Keys are re-exchanged every
   1 GiB / 2^28 packets by default (and whenever the peer asks); a peer that never completes a
   re-exchange hits the per-key packet stop instead of nonce reuse.
   Server-side command execution is a pure callback (`connection.CommandHandler`) — this module
   never spawns a process, so all sandboxing/privilege questions are the caller's. A handler that
   returns `error.CommandFailed` ends only its own channel (EOF, then CLOSE, no `exit-status`: the
   client sees a command that ended without one, Go's `ExitMissingError`); the connection keeps serving.
6. **Permanently out of scope:** TLS-anything (SSH doesn't use TLS), compression (`none` only), and
   any transport concern below the `std.Io.Reader`/`Writer` seam.

### Known limits of the userauth path (audited, deliberately not "fixed" here)

- **`AuthConfig.max_attempts` is a credential budget, not a time or packet budget.** Only a
  *rejected credential* consumes it (default 6). The RFC 4252 §7
  signature-less `publickey` *query* (answered SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK — by definition not an
  attempt) and a partial success do not, but every USERAUTH_REQUEST counts
  against `max_auth_requests` (128, Go's backstop), so a peer cannot loop on queries
  forever. SSH_MSG_IGNORE and SSH_MSG_DEBUG still cost nothing, so an unauthenticated peer can
  hold the pre-auth state machine open for as long as it keeps sending bytes. There is deliberately no
  OpenSSH-style `LoginGraceTime`: this module never owns the socket (see the transport-agnostic
  invariant above), so a read deadline can only be imposed by the caller that created the
  `std.Io.Reader`/`Writer`. **A server exposed to the internet must set one.**
- **The §7 query phase is a public-key-authorization oracle, by RFC design.** PK_OK-versus-FAILURE
  tells an unauthenticated peer whether a given public key blob is authorized for a given user
  name; OpenSSH answers the same question the same way. Relatedly, a *signed* request naming an
  unauthorized key is rejected by `AuthorizedKeyCheck` **before** any signature verification runs,
  so the two cases are also distinguishable by timing. Both leak strictly less than the protocol
  already grants, and closing either would mean diverging from RFC 4252 — so neither is treated as
  a defect. What is *not* leaked: every rejection is the same SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE, with the
  same continuation name-list and `partial success = false`, whatever the reason (unknown user,
  unknown method, unusable algorithm, blob-type mismatch, unauthorized key, bad signature).
- **The plaintext-password scrub is only observable in unsafe optimize modes.**
  `serveUserauth` `secureZero`s its packet scratch before freeing it, because the §8 password
  arrives in that buffer. In Debug/ReleaseSafe `std.mem.Allocator.free` already poisons the block
  with `undefined` (0xaa) and hides any omission; in ReleaseFast/ReleaseSmall that memset is
  elided and the scrub is the only thing standing between a successful login and the password
  persisting verbatim in freed heap. The regression test says so in its own comment.
- **`languages_client_to_server`/`languages_server_to_client` and `reserved` are decoded and never
  read.** Per RFC 4253 §7.1 the language name-lists are advisory (this module sends them empty) and
  `reserved` is "for future extension", sent as 0. Named here only because "decoded and discarded" is
  otherwise indistinguishable from an oversight.
- **Re-exchanges are not rate-limited.** A peer may start them as often as it likes, before
  authentication too (a CPU cost per exchange, as with OpenSSH).

## Verification

Run `scripts/modtest ssh` (Debug) or `zig build test-ssh`; the live-interop tests need `sshd`, `ssh` and
`ssh-keygen` and report `error.SkipZigTest` without them (they pick a random loopback port, so a port
collision can turn one live test into a skip on an individual run: a run with no skips is the one that
proves interop). `zig build interop-ssh` drives the Go `x/crypto/ssh` oracle (`tools/go_kbdint`, fetched by
`go run`, never vendored).

- **Wire codec:** `messages.zig` round-trips (string incl. empty, mpint incl. the high-bit zero-pad rule
  and zero, name-list incl. empty and the iterator over it) and `Cursor` bounds tests: a `0xffffffff`
  string length, an off-by-one length and a truncated length prefix are each `error.ProtocolError`.
- **Transport:** KEXINIT encode/decode, KDF formula, per-cipher packet round-trips and tamper detection,
  RFC 3526 prime bit-lengths, degenerate DH values, queued packets during a re-exchange and their
  sequence numbers, a re-exchange refusing a different host key, UNIMPLEMENTED handling, KEX messages
  outside an exchange refused, the guessing-server case (a discarded guess still counts a sequence
  number), the group-exchange cap (`gexGroupBitsOk` at the cap and one bit over).
- **Host/user keys:** `HostKey.fromOpenSSH` fixtures (ed25519, rsa, ecdsa P-256/384/521, and
  passphrase-protected ed25519 and ecdsa-p256) with `K_S` byte-compared against `ssh-keygen`'s `.pub`, ecdsa signature wire shape, error paths
  (a curve other than the expected one inside a well-formed ecdsa container, an Ed25519 seed that does
  not derive the container's public key, run in ReleaseFast), `out` zeroed on every parser error, the
  `zeroize` methods, fingerprints and `known_hosts` (hashed entries, `writeLine`) against `ssh-keygen`.
- **Userauth units:** `signedBlob` field order and framing, session-id sensitivity, the algorithm <->
  key-blob-type pairing table, the borrow-not-copy `sessionId` regression, crafted-wire oversize
  rejections, the freed-scratch password-scrub regression (observable only in unsafe optimize modes,
  see Known limits), and canned-stream units for both roles of the auth state machines (partial
  success, multi-round keyboard-interactive, abandoned dialogue, `none` under `no_client_auth`,
  `max_auth_requests`, `InvalidAuthConfig` cases, caller order, `retryable`, several keys with only the
  PK_OK'd one signed); Go's hooks (`sourceAddressAllowed` over addresses, blocks, mapped IPv4 and each
  refusal; a `source-address` grant refused for every method and at the `publickey` query;
  `publickey_verified` keeping, replacing and refusing a grant and never seeing a query or a bad
  signature; pre-auth and per-connection banners on the wire; the auth log of every verdict);
  `hostbased` both roles (`signedBlobHostbased` field order, a signature from another session, an
  unknown host, a mismatched or unsupported algorithm, the host-name bound); the client's password
  change (a refused new password asked again, a changer that gives up, the `max_password_changes`
  bound).
- **Loopback self-interop (`connection.zig`, `interop_test.zig`):** our client <-> our server over a real
  loopback socket, full stack: KEX, `publickey` (two-phase and direct), `password`, keyboard-interactive,
  partial-success chains, `hostbased`, session channel, `exec`, stdout/stderr/`exit-status`, and bulk output squeezed
  through a small window so window-adjust blocking happens in both directions.
- **Reject-teeth, each with a positive control through the same harness:** a signature bound to another
  session id, an unauthorized key, CHANNEL_OPEN before authentication (`ProtocolError` + DISCONNECT), a
  request after CLOSE, a window overrun, a chunk over the maximum packet size, a request for a channel
  never opened, a `direct-tcpip` open to the server (OPEN_FAILURE `unknown_channel_type`, byte-asserted),
  a second-factor mismatch, `max_attempts` ending a retrying client.
- **Live interop against OpenSSH, both directions:** our client against a spawned `sshd` and a real `ssh`
  against our server across the kex x cipher menu; publickey + `exec` (stdout, stderr and exit status
  asserted); the two RFC 8308 lanes, which are the only tests a foreign peer's algorithm choice can break
  (a real `ssh` with an RSA user key against our server, and our client with an RSA key against an
  `sshd` restricted to `rsa-sha2-512`; each fails only for its own half of the feature); strict KEX on
  and off, UNIMPLEMENTED, re-exchanges started by either side and by `rekey()`, concurrent sessions
  through `Connection`, pty-req + window-change, shell, `env` with `AcceptEnv`, signal -> exit-signal,
  `direct-tcpip`, `tcpip-forward` + `forwarded-tcpip`, a real `ssh` ControlMaster over one connection to
  `serveConnection`, `ssh -tt`, `SetEnv` filtered by `accept_env`; `AuthenticationMethods` chains
  (`publickey,publickey`, `publickey,password`); a real `ssh` answering our keyboard-interactive prompts
  through `SSH_ASKPASS_REQUIRE=force`; a real `ssh` shown our pre-auth and per-connection banners and
  logging in under a `source-address` grant it meets, and refused by one it does not; the Go oracle for keyboard-interactive and for
  `PartialSuccessError`, with a wrong second answer refused.
- **Fuzz** (`SSH_FUZZ=<runs>[,<first seed>]`, testkit's deterministic driver, ReleaseSafe; never
  `zig build --fuzz`): `ssh-readstring`, `ssh-readmpint`, `ssh-kexinit`, `ssh-readpacket`,
  `ssh-keyload`, `ssh-pubkey`, `ssh-userauth` (both roles over one stream, with corpus seeds and reach
  labels: hostbased requests with valid, refused and cut-off signatures, `publickey` grants carrying an
  attacker-chosen `source-address` list, the client's `PasswordChanger` answering CHANGEREQ streams),
  `ssh-sourceaddr` (`sourceAddressAllowed` over built and raw lists and every peer shape, against a
  masked-compare model) and `ssh-session`. The card's Hardening line has the budget.
- **Constant time (ctgrind):** rows `dh` (the montint kernel; the remaining contexts are the mpint length
  of `e`/`K`, inherent to RFC 4251), `gex`, `ecdh` (`fromScalar` declassifies only its zero verdict) and
  `pem` (the host-key PEM decode on the ed25519 fixture), with positive controls `ffpow` (the old
  `std.crypto.ff` path) and `pemstd` (the old std base64 path) that must keep finding contexts; rows,
  counts and attribution live in `scripts/checks/ctgrind-expected.tsv`. The packet-MAC compares have no
  ctgrind target (unobservable).
- **Stack residue:** `stackprobe_test.zig` (ReleaseFast) checks every key type and every KEX method and
  role for zero residue; `stackprobe2_test.zig` replays a peer's transcript from a fixed reader to measure
  `connectInto`, `serverHandshake` and `serverKexRound`, the container parsers, `writePacket` under
  chacha20-poly1305 and AES-GCM, `deriveKeys`, and the keyboard-interactive and prompted-password paths.
  A burn site covered by another burn is measured by switching both off together.
- **Mutation:** whole-module mutants over `transport`, `server`, `userauth`, `connection`, `messages`,
  `keys` and `knownhosts` (N mutants behind a runtime switch, W wipe/burn sites switched in `burn.zig`,
  constant-time mutants measured with ctgrind); every survivor became a killing test or an argued
  equivalent/unobservable verdict. No defect was found in a MAC, signature, host-key, strict-KEX, userauth
  or `known_hosts` check.
- **Audit:** the card's `**Audit:**` line is the current score, cumulative over the last whole-module
  mutation run and the delta runs after it.
- **No curve25519 KAT:** RFC 8731 publishes no curve25519-sha256 test vectors (its §5 is IANA
  considerations only), so there is no independent known-answer test to wire; the KEX is anchored by the
  live interop lanes.

## Build options

Consumer build options (CONVENTIONS §4.2), added 2026-10-18:

| option | values | default | `-Dprofile=small` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ssh-gex-max-bits` | 4096..8192, multiple of 1024 | 8192 (Go's maximum, graded) | 4096 |

- **Lower cap:** the client's `SSH_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_REQUEST` asks for at most the cap, and a server group above it fails the key
  exchange with `error.KexFailed` (`gexGroupBitsOk`, tested at the cap and one bit over); `GexMod = DynModint(cap)` carries
  no montint slot above it. It is the same type as rsa's `DynModint` at the same cap, so an application lowering both
  (`-Dprofile=small` does) loses every 8192-bit kernel.
- **What it buys** (size probe `tools/sizeprobe.zig`: `GexMod` + one `gexPow`; ReleaseSmall, native ADX/BMI2 x86_64,
  stripped): `-Dssh-gex-max-bits=4096` alone 184 720 → 115 160 B; `-Dprofile=small` (with montint's looped kernel)
  → 29 440 B.
- **What the consumer loses:** group exchange with a server that will only offer a group above the cap (OpenSSH's moduli
  file goes to 8192; a server picks the group closest to the client's preferred 2048, so this is rare). `curve25519`,
  `ecdh-*`, `mlkem768x25519` and the fixed MODP groups are unaffected.

## What is deliberately not done

- **Compression** (`none` only), and TLS-anything: SSH does not use TLS. Transport concerns below the
  `std.Io.Reader`/`Writer` seam are the caller's.
- **X11 forwarding, agent forwarding, server-side TCP/IP forwarding** (`direct-tcpip` opens and
  `tcpip-forward` global requests are refused with `unknown_channel_type` / REQUEST_FAILURE): honouring
  them means the server opening or listening on sockets, which this module never does. A server-side
  `signal` is acknowledged and dropped (a one-shot handler has nothing to deliver it to) and the server
  never sends `exit-signal`.
- **Server-side stdin as a pipe.** `CommandHandler` is a one-shot function, so `ServeConfig.stdin_mode`
  chooses between buffering CHANNEL_DATA until the client's EOF (`.collect_until_eof`, the default) and
  running at once with empty stdin (`.ignore`); streaming would need a different handler shape (see the
  Go-parity item in the Backlog).
- **A `LoginGraceTime`:** the module never owns the socket, so a read deadline can only be imposed by the
  caller that created the reader and writer.
- **RFC 8308 extensions sent by the client.** The client advertises `ext-info-c` and accepts a server's
  `SSH_MSG_EXT_INFO` but sends none: `delay-compression` needs compression, `no-flow-control`
  contradicts the §5.2 window accounting, and `elevation` is Windows-specific.
- **Bare `ssh-rsa` (SHA-1) and the other legacy algorithms** (CBC, HMAC-SHA1, DSA) as defaults: legacy
  names would be explicit opt-ins in the `supported_*` lists, never on by default (see Backlog).
- **Three LOW review findings, kept as Go's `x/crypto/ssh` (the reference) behaves:** `Server.sendData`
  sees an SSH_MSG_DISCONNECT only while it waits for window space, otherwise at the next read (blocking
  I/O on a socket this module does not own: a peer that hung up fails the next write or read, as in Go);
  the client `Session` keeps data the server sends after its EOF (Go's `handleData` does not check EOF
  either; OpenSSH drops it); a CHANNEL_OPEN_CONFIRMATION with a zero maximum packet size is
  `error.ChannelOpenFailed` without a CLOSE to the server (Go returns its error the same way).
- **The §8 password-change sub-protocol, server side.** `serveUserauth` never sends
  SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_PASSWD_CHANGEREQ and refuses a change request as a wrong password: `sshd` does the
  same (`auth2-passwd.c` logs "password change not supported" and fails the attempt) and Go's server
  refuses one outright. The client half is implemented.
- **`hostbased` against OpenSSH, live.** Not tested: a real `ssh` signs hostbased requests only
  through the setuid `ssh-keysign` with `EnableSSHKeysign` in the system `ssh_config`, and `sshd`
  reads `shosts.equiv`/`~/.shosts` and `ssh_known_hosts` from fixed paths; neither can be arranged
  without root or the user's home. Our client and server are tested against each other and the
  signed blob field by field.
- **`@cert-authority` known_hosts lines as trust anchors** (they need certificates), Go's
  `KeyError.Want` host-key-algorithm preference and the `CheckHostIP` second lookup by address.

## Backlog / deferred

None open.

## Roadmap

- **Go `x/crypto/ssh` parity, phase P3** (owner goal: "our ssh qualitatively at the level of the Go
  implementation"): a server API in Go's shape (channels and requests handed to the application, which
  also lifts the batch-handler and server-side `signal`/`exit-signal` limits), streamlocal, a `Signer` +
  `ssh-agent` client, OpenSSH certificates (`*-cert-v01@openssh.com`, user and host; `@cert-authority`
  in `known_hosts` follows), GSSAPI, and the legacy opt-ins (Go's `Insecure*`: DSA, CBC/3DES, RC4,
  DH-sha1, `ssh-rsa` SHA-1; the lists are runtime-configurable and a legacy name would live only in the
  `supported_*` ceiling, off by default). Older network gear that offers only CTR/HMAC-SHA1 is the use
  case. Effort: small-medium for certificates and the agent client, each.
  Size: months in total (a server API in Go's shape, an agent client, certificates, GSSAPI, the legacy opt-ins: each its own piece with Go/OpenSSH interop tests).
- **SFTP client** (draft-ietf-secsh-filexfer-02 v3). File transfer is the other reason people use SSH from a
  library (russh and libssh2 have it). It would be its own module on top of `subsystem`; no sibling exists.
  Effort: large. Fits the scope.
  Size: weeks (a new module over `subsystem`, draft-02 v3 packets, OpenSSH sftp-server interop).

## Anchoring

**Anchor grade:** class A · oracle MIXED

- **Class A** — wire/interop format — other implementations must byte-agree with it.
- **Oracle MIXED** — anchored for some paths, self for others — the evidence below names which.

**What the tests actually contain.** self loopback client<->server baseline; live OpenSSH interop (both roles) and Go x/crypto/ssh (keyboard-interactive) — skip when the peer is absent

**How it got there.** No external oracle exists for what remains. self-loopback can't be anchored by construction; real anchor already lives in OpenSSH interop
